title: Esther 9:20–32
context: Mordecai records these events and writes to all the Jews to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year as days of feasting, gladness, sending food to one another, and gifts to the needy, because their sorrow was turned to gladness (9:20–22). The narrator recounts Haman’s plot and the casting of Pur, “that is the lot” (9:24), and explains that the festival is called Purim from that word (9:26). The Jews bind themselves, their descendants, and all who join them to keep these days in every generation (9:27–28). Esther and Mordecai then send a second letter with full authority to confirm Purim, including matters of fasting and mourning (9:29–32; compare 4:3, 16). The book does not name God in establishing the festival. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s people rightly remember deliverance with joy, generosity, and care for the poor.

verses.text: Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, both near and far,
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai writes these things and sends letters to all the Jews in all the provinces. Arminian readers note that Mordecai takes responsibility for preserving the memory of what happened. Writing ensures that the deliverance will not be forgotten.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the value of written remembrance for the community. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the beginning of the formal establishment of Purim, and both affirm the importance of remembering God’s people’s deliverance across generations.

verses.text: to enjoin them that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar yearly,
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai instructs them to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year. Arminian readers note that the observance includes both dates, honoring the experience of the provinces and of Susa. The festival is meant to be lasting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the annual observance and its roots in the events of 9:17–18. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as establishing a recurring festival of remembrance and see no doctrinal dispute in its dates.

verses.text: as the days in which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned to them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending presents of food to one another, and gifts to the needy.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the days when the Jews had rest from their enemies and the month turned from sorrow to gladness; they are to feast and send food to one another and gifts to the needy. Arminian readers note that joy overflows in care for the poor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see thanksgiving expressed through generosity, and many discern God’s hand in the turning from sorrow to gladness, though the text does not name him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of grateful remembrance that includes the needy.

verses.text: The Jews accepted the custom that they had begun, as Mordecai had written to them,
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews accept the custom they had begun, as Mordecai had written. Arminian readers note that the people embrace the festival willingly. The observance is not simply imposed; it grows from their own experience and response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the community taking up the custom as its own. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a people who freely adopt a practice of remembrance, and both see in it a healthy pattern for communal celebration.

verses.text: because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast “Pur”, that is the lot, to consume them and to destroy them;
verses.arminianNotes: Haman the Agagite, enemy of all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them and had cast Pur, “that is the lot,” to consume them. Arminian readers note that the narrator retells the story briefly to explain the festival. The lot, meant for destruction, gives its name to deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the lot cast in 3:7 and, with many readers, see God’s hidden rule over it, though the book itself does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the festival’s origin, without decoding the lot beyond the narrator’s own words.

verses.text: but when this became known to the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked plan, which he had planned against the Jews, should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
verses.arminianNotes: When the matter became known to the king, he commanded that Haman’s wicked plan return on his own head, and that he and his sons be hanged. Arminian readers note the justice of the outcome: the plotter falls into the trap he set for others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a just reversal, in which evil rebounds on the one who planned it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summary of the story’s justice and decline to add details beyond the narrator’s summary of chapters 7–9.

verses.text: Therefore they called these days “Purim”, from the word “Pur.” Therefore because of all the words of this letter, and of that which they had seen concerning this matter, and that which had come to them,
verses.arminianNotes: The days are called Purim, from the word Pur. Because of the letter and what they had seen and experienced, the Jews establish the observance. Arminian readers note that the name keeps the story alive, linking the festival to the lot Haman cast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the name as a lasting reminder of the reversal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as explaining the name and grounds of the festival, and both affirm that remembering deliverance by name helps each generation recall what happened.

verses.text: the Jews established and imposed on themselves, on their descendants, and on all those who joined themselves to them, so that it should not fail that they would keep these two days according to what was written and according to its appointed time every year;
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews bind themselves, their descendants, and all who join them to keep these two days every year. Arminian readers note the inclusion of those who join the Jews, echoing 8:17. The festival is open to all who become part of the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the binding commitment and its extension to newcomers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a solemn communal pledge to remember deliverance and see in it the welcome of outsiders into the people’s celebration.

verses.text: and that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and that these days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews, nor their memory perish from their offspring.
verses.arminianNotes: These days are to be remembered in every generation, family, province, and city, and Purim is never to fail among the Jews. Arminian readers note the emphasis on lasting memory. Each generation must take up the remembrance for itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the importance of passing on the memory of deliverance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a call to faithful remembrance across generations and affirm that God’s people should not forget how they were preserved.

verses.text: Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter of Purim.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther the queen and Mordecai write with full authority to confirm this second letter of Purim. Arminian readers note that Esther, who risked her life for her people, now joins in establishing their remembrance. Her authority confirms the custom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Esther and Mordecai together confirming the festival. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the establishment of Purim through those who led the deliverance, and both note the prominence given to Esther here.

verses.text: He sent letters to all the Jews in the hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus with words of peace and truth,
verses.arminianNotes: Letters go to all the Jews in the 127 provinces with words of peace and truth. Arminian readers note the gracious tone of the letters. The establishment of Purim is communicated in a spirit of peace, not merely as a command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the words of peace and truth. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a message that strengthens the community and affirm that peace and truth belong together in the life of God’s people.

verses.text: to confirm these days of Purim in their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had decreed, and as they had imposed upon themselves and their descendants in the matter of the fastings and their mourning.
verses.arminianNotes: The letters confirm Purim in its appointed times, as Mordecai and Esther decreed, including matters of fasting and mourning. Arminian readers note that the remembrance includes the earlier sorrow (compare 4:3, 16), not only the joy that followed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the festival holding together lament and gladness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking Purim to the fasting of chapter 4, and both affirm that remembering deliverance includes remembering the danger and grief that preceded it.

verses.text: The commandment of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther’s command confirms the matters of Purim, and it is written in the book. Arminian readers note that the written record gives the festival lasting authority. Esther’s role in confirming it is honored to the end of the account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the written confirmation and Esther’s authority. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the close of the account of Purim’s establishment and affirm the value of preserving such remembrance in writing.
